scenes.text: Spilling coffee on yourself can make people like you more, but only if they already think you're great.
Psychologists call this the pratfall effect.
In nineteen sixty-six, Elliot Aronson and two colleagues put it to the test.
Forty-eight male students at the University of Minnesota listened to a recording.
It was supposedly a student trying out for a college quiz bowl team, facing fifty hard questions.
In one version, he answered ninety-two percent of the hard questions correctly.
He was also an honor student and yearbook editor.
In another version, he got only thirty percent right and sounded completely average.
Then, on some tapes, you hear a crash as he spills coffee all over his new suit.
Afterward, an interviewer asked each student how much they liked him.
The brilliant contestant who spilled the coffee was rated the most likable of all.
But the average contestant who spilled it was rated the least likable.
The idea is that a small blunder makes an impressive person seem more human.
For someone who already seems ordinary, it just looks like one more mistake.
Have you ever liked someone more after they messed up? Tell me below.

title: Why a clumsy mistake can make people like you more ☕
caption: In a 1966 study, a near-perfect quiz contestant who spilled coffee on himself was rated the most likable. The same blunder made an average contestant the least liked.
